issues.legal_issue: An ancestral estate that is impartible by custom and devolves by primogeniture remains joint family property for purposes of the junior members’ rights of maintenance and survivorship.
material_facts: The estate was impartible by custom and had passed as an ancestral estate through primogeniture.
The deed described the eldest son as succeeding to the estate and the younger sons as having a right to maintenance and a reasonable share in lieu of that right.
issues.conclusion: The estate was not the holder’s separate or exclusive property: although partition and restraint of alienation were inconsistent with its impartibility, the rights of maintenance and survivorship remained, and the junior members’ maintenance right was based on their joint ownership.
issues.legal_principle: Under Shiba Prasad Singh v. Rani Prayag Kumari Devi, an ancestral impartible estate held by succession through primogeniture is part of the undivided Hindu family estate. Rani Sartaj Kuari v. Deoraj Kuari and the First Pittapur case establish that the rights to partition and to restrain alienations do not apply in the ordinary way to an impartible estate. Collector of Gorakhpur v. Ram Sunder Mal and Baijnath Prasad Singh v. Tej Bali Singh affirm that maintenance and survivorship remain and that junior members’ maintenance right rests on joint ownership; survivorship is distinct from a mere spes successionis and can be surrendered. The Court also referred to Raja Yarlagadda Mallikarjuna Prasad Nayadu v. Raja Yarlagadda Durga Prasad Nayadu and Protap Chandra Deo v. Jagadish Chandra Deo.

predicates.impartible_estate_dispute: The proceeding concerns an estate that is impartible under custom.
predicates.ancestral_estate: The holder received the estate as ancestral property.
predicates.holder_succeeded_by_primogeniture: The holder succeeded to the ancestral estate by primogeniture.

issues.definition: When a dispute concerns a customarily impartible ancestral estate inherited by primogeniture, junior family members retain rights of maintenance and survivorship.

issues.legal_issue: A transfer of estate property to a junior family member in settlement of a customary maintenance right, without money consideration, is not a sale or gift for rehabilitation-grant assessment.
material_facts: A holder of an impartible estate executed a deed transferring property to his younger brother.
The deed stated that younger sons had a customary right to maintenance and that the property was provided in lieu of that right.
The deed provided for possession by the recipient and his male descendants, with reversion if that line ended, and did not provide for money consideration.
The State challenged recognition of the transfer in an appeal concerning the recipient’s rehabilitation grant.
issues.conclusion: The deed was a settlement in lieu of the recipient’s obligatory maintenance right, not a sale or gift, and was not excluded from recognition for assessing the rehabilitation grant.
issues.legal_principle: Section 23(1) of the U.P. Zamindari Abolition and Land Reforms Act, 1950 bars recognition for rehabilitation-grant assessment of transfers by way of sale or gift within its scope. Sections 73 and 79 concern rehabilitation grants and the application for their determination. Applying the principles concerning the joint-family character of an ancestral impartible estate and the junior members’ maintenance rights, the Court held that this settlement in lieu of maintenance was neither a sale nor a gift within section 23(1).

rule.if: grant_assessment_appeal and transfer_to_junior_family_member and transfer_in_lieu_of_customary_maintenance and no_money_consideration

predicates.grant_assessment_appeal: The proceeding is an appeal about whether transferred property may be recognized in assessing a rehabilitation grant.
predicates.transfer_to_junior_family_member: The holder of an impartible estate transferred property to a junior member of the family.
predicates.transfer_in_lieu_of_customary_maintenanc: The deed stated that the property was transferred in settlement of the recipient’s customary maintenance right.
predicates.no_money_consideration: The transfer was not made in exchange for money consideration.

issues.definition: In a rehabilitation-grant appeal, a transfer to a junior family member in settlement of customary maintenance, without money consideration, is not disqualified from grant assessment as a sale or gift.

issues.legal_issue: A grant determination need not be remanded for failure to frame formal issues or take evidence when no disputed question of fact was raised and the challenge presents only a question of law.
material_facts: The State sought a remand, arguing that the grant officer had not treated the application and objection as pleadings, framed issues, or taken evidence as in a civil suit.
The State had not disputed the customary maintenance right in its written objection.
No disputed question of fact was raised before the grant officer, and the challenge concerned a question of law.
issues.conclusion: Remand was not warranted because there were no disputed factual questions requiring issues or evidence.
issues.legal_principle: The Court held that the asserted procedural irregularities did not require a remand where the written objection raised no disputed question of fact and the award was challenged only on a question of law. No earlier case or statutory provision was relied on for this procedural conclusion.

rule.if: grant_determination_appeal and formal_issues_or_evidence_omitted and no_disputed_factual_issue and challenge_only_legal

predicates.grant_determination_appeal: The proceeding is an appeal challenging a determination made on a rehabilitation-grant application.
predicates.formal_issues_or_evidence_omitted: The decision-maker did not frame formal issues or take evidence in the manner used in a civil suit.
predicates.no_disputed_factual_issue: The objection raised no disputed question of fact requiring evidence.
predicates.challenge_only_legal: The challenge to the determination presented only a question of law.

issues.definition: In an appeal concerning a grant determination, omission of formal issues or evidence does not require remand when no factual dispute was raised and the challenge is only legal.
